The plan is clear, well-structured, and backed by real traction, but several improvements would make the submission more credible and persuasive.

1) Fix the financial logic and make it verifiable. The numbers do not reconcile: four pilots generated $41,500 (about $10,400 per school, which sits between the $9,500 and $18,000 packages), yet the projection of 12 schools yields only ~$190,000 (about $15,800 each) with no explanation of mix between packages. Also, 30 schools at 18,000 would be 540,000, but the plan says 520,000. Add a simple revenue build (customers by package type, renewals, churn), a cost build (coach cost per school, hours per cycle, dashboard/software, travel), and a monthly or quarterly cash view. Clarify that 'profitable on paper' excludes founder salaries and any real coach labor costs, and explain how a 60% gross margin is calculated (coach hours x pay rate). Show the break-even logic rather than just asserting it.

2) Show unit economics and delivery capacity. Three cycles x three workshops per cycle is nine coaching sessions plus analysis and briefs per school. Quantify hours per school and how many schools one coach can serve. With three students doing this part time and 12-60 schools projected, capacity, hiring timeline, and quality control are the key scaling risks. Also address customer acquisition cost and sales cycle length, since selling to school leaders is slow and tied to budget calendars.

3) Strengthen the evidence of impact. The central claim is that students actually move on targeted standards, yet no results from the pilots are reported. Include pre/post data, a case study, or testimonials with specifics (e.g., percent growth on targeted standards versus comparison groups), and note limitations honestly. Clarify the status of the two schools that 'want' to renew: get letters of intent or signed commitments. Disclose who the four pilot customers are (or anonymized details), how they were acquired, and whether pilots were discounted.

4) Tighten the market sizing and justify assumptions. The TAM is a simple top-down multiplication (3,500 x $18,000) with no source for the 3,500 figure or the claim that this segment lacks analytics support. Cite sources, and add a bottom-up SAM/SOM focused on the home state (140 small charters) with realistic win rates and a path from there to other states. Address state-by-state variation in assessments, standards, and charter regulations, which affects the template library and expansion.

5) Deepen the competitive and defensibility analysis. Name specific competitors (e.g., software platforms, regional consulting/PD providers, instructional coaching nonprofits, district-offered services) and compare on price, offering, and evidence. The line that a bigger firm could copy them but they have a head start is weak. Explain what is truly defensible: proprietary templates, accumulated cross-school data, switching costs, outcomes track record, or relationships, and how they will deepen those over time.

6) Address risks and operational realities. Cover student data privacy and compliance (FERPA, state laws, data-sharing agreements), since they ingest student assessment exports; who owns the data; and security practices. Discuss reliance on three part-time student founders, what happens with graduation and academic schedules, whether founders will commit full time, and equity/ownership splits and any IP agreements with the university. Note that the team lacks a dedicated sales or operations/finance leader and explain how advisors will fill gaps; consider quantifying advisor involvement.

7) Make the ask specific. The prize amount is not stated, and use of funds is described only qualitatively. Provide a budget with dollar allocations (two part-time coaches, dashboard development, travel), expected milestones those funds unlock, and metrics for success at 6 and 12 months. Explain why the claim of doubling customers within a year follows from the spending.

8) Clean up writing and presentation. Fix typos and informal phrasing ('alot', 'thru', 'what we heard again and again'), reduce repeated assertions, and lead with a crisp one-sentence value proposition and the traction headline (four paying schools, $41,500) rather than burying it late. Add a few concrete visuals: a one-page customer journey, a pricing table, a revenue projection chart, and a simple dashboard screenshot. Support interview findings (31 leaders and teachers) with a few quantified takeaways. Finally, ensure claims like 'we are profitable' and 'break even by mid-year two' are stated with the assumptions behind them.
